title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
hook: he turns toward Jerusalem, and the foxes have holes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve sent out with nothing, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was nothing for the journey. What did you leave behind? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Halfway through Luke's Gospel, the whole book turns. Until now Jesus has been moving around Galilee, the lake, the villages, the hills. Then, in one verse, he turns south. From here on, for ten chapters, Luke tells everything as part of a single long walk toward Jerusalem, the city where he knows he will suffer. Scholars call it the travel narrative. The road takes up more of Luke than any other single section. And the very first thing that happens on it is a door slammed in his face. Today, the turn.
screen: `HALFWAY THROUGH, THE BOOK TURNS.` → `TEN CHAPTERS OF ONE LONG WALK.` → `A DOOR SLAMS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the hinge in the Douay-Rheims: "And it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were accomplishing, that he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." Assumption here means his being taken up, to the cross and to the Father. To set your face is an old Hebrew way of speaking: to fix your direction and refuse to be turned. Isaiah's servant says he has set his face like a flint. Jesus sends messengers ahead into a Samaritan village, and the village won't receive him, because he's headed for Jerusalem. James and John are furious. They ask if they should call fire down from heaven. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they simply go on to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you wherever you go. Jesus answers: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Know what you're signing up for. The second says, let me first go and bury my father. The third says, let me first say goodbye at home. And Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Anyone who has plowed knows why. If you look over your shoulder, the furrow wanders. These sayings are hard, and Luke doesn't soften them. Catholic readers have usually heard them not as contempt for family, which the commandments honor, but as a question of what comes first. Jesus has set his face. He asks the people walking beside him to set theirs.
screen: `THE DAYS OF HIS ASSUMPTION.` · `NO FIRE ON THE SAMARITAN VILLAGE.` · `THE FOXES HAVE HOLES.` · `A HAND ON THE PLOW.` · then, large: `HE STEADFASTLY SET HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: commit to one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been circling: a conversation you keep postponing, a habit you keep almost starting, a decision you keep reopening. Pick one. Now picture yourself setting your face toward it, the way you'd turn to walk a road. What's the first step, today? Name it. Notice the urge to look back, the reasons to wait. Let them be there, and keep facing forward. If you pray, ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
He set his face. Luke's hinge: Jesus fixes his direction toward Jerusalem and the cross, and won't be turned. Today's word.
Your line: no looking back. Today, take the first step on your one hard thing, and when you want to turn around, keep your hand on the plow. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this passage at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and it is often read when men and women discern a vocation to priesthood or religious life.

trapdoor: what you thought: he set his face means he looked determined.
what it means: it's a Hebrew idiom for fixing your direction and refusing to turn, and here it means toward the cross.
what a scholar hears: Luke's travel narrative runs from 9:51 to about 19:28; the phrase echoes Isaiah 50:7, I have set my face as a flint.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 9:51, 9:58 and 9:62.
'The road takes up more of Luke than any other single section' is a softened version of a common observation about the travel narrative (9:51–19:28); confirm.
Isaiah 50:7 'set my face as a flint' is paraphrased in the voice; the trapdoor wording follows the common KJV/Douay sense. Confirm.
Reading 'let the dead bury their dead' (9:60) is omitted; confirm the gentle framing of the family sayings fits Catholic teaching.
